verses.33:21: His flesh wastes away out of sight, and his bones that were not seen are laid bare.
verses.33:22: And his soul comes near to the pit, and his life to those who put to death.
verses.33:23: If there is an angel for him, a mediator, one out of a thousand, to declare to a man his uprightness,
verses.33:24: then he is gracious to him and says, 'Rescue him from going down to the pit; I have found a ransom.'
verses.33:25: His flesh grows fresher than in youth; he returns to the days of his youthful strength.
verses.33:26: He prays to God, and He is pleased with him; he sees His face with joyful shouting, and He restores to a mortal his righteousness.
verses.33:27: He sings before people and says, 'I sinned and perverted what was upright, yet it was not paid back to me.'
verses.33:28: He has redeemed his soul from passing into the pit, and his life will see the light.
verses.33:29: Look, God performs all these things, twice, three times, with a man,
verses.33:30: to restore his soul from the pit, to be illuminated with the light of life.
verses.33:31: Give heed, Job, listen to me; keep silent, and I myself will speak.
verses.33:32: If you have words, reply to me; speak, for I desire to declare you righteous.
verses.33:33: If not, you yourself listen to me; keep silent, and I will teach you wisdom."
verses.34:2: "Listen to my words, you wise men, and you who have knowledge, give ear to me.
verses.34:3: For the ear tests words, just as the palate tastes when eating.
verses.34:4: Let us choose justice for ourselves; let us discern among us what is good.
verses.34:5: For Job has said, 'I am righteous, yet God has set aside my right.
verses.34:6: Am I to lie against my right? My arrow wound is incurable, without transgression.'
verses.34:7: What man is there like Job, who drinks mockery like water,
verses.34:8: and journeys in fellowship with workers of iniquity, and walks with men of wickedness?
verses.34:9: For he said, 'A man does not benefit when he takes delight with God.'
verses.34:10: Therefore, men of discernment, listen to me: far be wickedness from God, and injustice from the Almighty.
verses.34:11: For He repays a person his deed, and according to a man's path He causes it to find him.
verses.34:12: Indeed, truly God will not act wickedly, and the Almighty will not distort justice.
verses.34:13: Who entrusted the earth to Him, and who placed the entire world upon Him?
verses.34:14: If He should set His heart toward Himself, and gather His spirit and His breath to Himself,
verses.34:15: all flesh would expire together, and humanity would return to dust.
verses.34:16: And if you have understanding, listen to this; give ear to the sound of my words.
verses.34:17: Can one who hates justice truly govern? Or will you condemn the righteous, mighty One—
verses.34:18: should one say to a king, 'Worthless!' or 'Wicked!' to nobles?—
verses.34:19: who shows no favoritism to princes and does not regard the wealthy ahead of the poor, since all of them are the work of His hands?
verses.34:20: In an instant they die, and at midnight the people are convulsed and pass away, and the mighty one is removed by no hand.
verses.34:21: For His eyes are over the ways of a man, and He sees all his footsteps.
verses.34:22: There is no darkness and there is no deep gloom where workers of iniquity can hide themselves.
verses.34:23: For He does not set His attention further upon a man, for him to go to God in judgment.
verses.34:24: He shatters mighty men without inquiry, and stations others in their place.
verses.34:25: Therefore He recognizes their deeds, and He overturns them by night so they are crushed.
verses.34:26: As wicked men He strikes them in the place of onlookers,
verses.34:27: because they turned away from following Him and paid no heed to any of His ways,
verses.34:28: so as to bring to Him the outcry of the poor, and He hears the outcry of the afflicted.
verses.34:29: Yet when He remains silent, who can condemn? And when He hides His face, who can look upon Him, whether toward a nation or toward a person alike?—
verses.34:30: so that a godless person may not reign, nor those who are snares to the people.
verses.34:31: For has anyone said to God, 'I have endured; I will not act corruptly.
verses.34:32: Beyond what I see, You teach me; if I have committed injustice, I will not repeat it'?
verses.34:33: Is He to repay it on your terms, since you have rejected it? For it is you who will choose, and not I; so speak what you know.
verses.34:34: Men of discernment will say to me, and a wise man who listens to me:
verses.34:35: 'Job does not speak with knowledge, and his words have no insight.'
verses.34:36: If only Job were tested to the very end, because of his answers like those of men of iniquity;
verses.34:37: for he adds transgression to his sin; among us he claps his hands, and he multiplies his sayings against God."
verses.35:2: "Do you consider this to be justice, that you have said, 'My righteousness is greater than that of God'?
verses.35:3: For you say, 'What does it benefit you? What do I gain more than from my sin?'
verses.35:4: I will answer you with words, and your companions with you.
verses.35:5: Look toward the heavens and see, and gaze upon the clouds; they are higher than you.
verses.35:6: If you sin, what can you effect against Him? And if your transgressions grow many, what can you do to Him?
verses.35:7: If you are righteous, what can you give Him, or what will He take from your hand?
verses.35:8: Your wickedness affects a man like you, and your righteousness a son of man.
verses.35:9: From the multitude of oppressions they raise an outcry; they cry out for help from the arm of the powerful.
verses.35:10: Yet not one says, 'Where is God, the One who made me, who gives songs during the night,
verses.35:11: who instructs us more than the animals of the earth, and more than the birds of the heavens makes us wise?'
verses.35:12: There they cry out, yet He does not respond, because of the arrogance of evil people.
verses.35:13: Indeed, God will not hear an empty outcry, and the Almighty will not look upon it.
verses.35:14: How much less when you say you cannot look upon Him! Judgment lies before Him, so wait for Him.
verses.35:15: And now, because His anger has not punished, and He has not greatly taken note of insolence,
verses.35:16: Job opens wide his mouth in emptiness; with no knowledge he multiplies words."
verses.36:2: "Wait for me a little while, and I will inform you, for there are still words on behalf of God.
verses.36:3: I will bring my knowledge from afar, and I will attribute righteousness to my Maker.
verses.36:4: For truly my words are not falsehood; one complete in knowledge is with you.
verses.36:5: Look, God is mighty and does not despise anyone; He is mighty in strength of heart.
verses.36:6: He does not preserve the wicked alive, but He grants justice to the afflicted.
verses.36:7: He does not take His eyes off the righteous; rather, with kings on the throne He seats them forever, and they are lifted high.
verses.36:8: And if they are bound in shackles, captured in ropes of affliction,
verses.36:9: then He declares to them their deed and their transgressions, that they have behaved proudly.
verses.36:10: He opens their ear to discipline and says that they must turn back from iniquity.
verses.36:11: If they listen and serve Him, they will finish their days in well-being and their years in delights.
verses.36:12: But if they do not listen, they will pass away by the sword and expire without knowledge.
verses.36:13: Yet the godless in heart harbor anger; they do not cry out for help when He binds them.
verses.36:14: Their soul dies in youth, and their life ends among the shrine prostitutes.
verses.36:15: He rescues the afflicted in his affliction and opens their ear in oppression.
verses.36:16: Moreover, He lured you from the mouth of distress—in place of it, a broad space with no confinement—and what rested on your table was full of rich food.
verses.36:17: Yet you are full of the judgment on the wicked; judgment and justice take hold.
verses.36:18: For there is wrath—watch that it does not lure you into scoffing, and do not let the magnitude of a ransom turn you aside.
verses.36:19: Will your cry for help suffice so that you are not in distress, or all the exertions of strength?
verses.36:20: Do not yearn for the night, when peoples disappear where they stand.
verses.36:21: Guard yourself—do not turn toward iniquity, for you have chosen this over affliction.
verses.36:22: Look, God is exalted in His strength; who is an instructor like Him?
verses.36:23: Who has assigned His way to Him, and who has said, 'You have committed injustice'?
verses.36:24: Remember to magnify His work, of which people have sung.
verses.36:25: All mankind has gazed upon it; mortal man looks on from afar.
verses.36:26: See, God is great, and we do not know Him; the number of His years is beyond searching.
verses.36:27: For He draws up drops of water; out of His mist they distill as rain,
verses.36:28: which the skies pour out; they shower upon mankind in abundance.
verses.36:29: Moreover, can anyone understand the spreadings of the thick clouds, the roarings of His canopy?
verses.36:30: Look, He spreads out His lightning around Himself, and He covers the roots of the sea.
verses.36:31: For through them He judges peoples; He supplies food in abundance.
verses.36:32: He covers His palms with lightning and commands it to hit the target.
verses.36:33: Its crashing tells of Him; the livestock also tell of what is rising."
verses.37:1: "At this too my heart quakes and springs out of its place.
verses.37:2: Listen intently to the raging of His voice and the rumble that goes out from His mouth.
verses.37:3: Beneath all the heavens He releases it, and His lightning to the edges of the earth.
verses.37:4: After it a voice roars; He thunders with the voice of His majesty, and He does not hold them back when His voice is heard.
verses.37:5: God thunders marvelously with His voice, performing great things that we do not know.
verses.37:6: For He says to the snow, 'Fall upon the earth,' and also to the downpour of rain, even the downpour of His mighty rains.
verses.37:7: He puts a seal on the hand of every person, so that all the people of His making may know.
verses.37:8: Then the wild animals enter a lair and dwell in their dens.
verses.37:9: Out of the chamber comes the storm wind, and out of the scattering winds comes the cold.
verses.37:10: From the breath of God ice is produced, and the breadth of the waters is frozen solid.
verses.37:11: Indeed, He weighs down the thick cloud with moisture; He scatters the cloud of His lightning.
verses.37:12: It turns about in circuits by His direction, so that they carry out everything He commands them across the face of the inhabited earth.
verses.37:13: Whether for a rod, or for His land, or for steadfast love, He brings it about.
verses.37:14: Give ear to this, Job; stand still and ponder the marvels of God.
verses.37:15: Do you know how God lays His charge upon them and makes the lightning of His cloud flash forth?
verses.37:16: Do you know about the balancings of the thick clouds, the marvels of the One complete in knowledge,
verses.37:17: you whose clothes are hot when the earth lies still from the south?
verses.37:18: Can you beat out the skies with Him, firm as a cast mirror?
verses.37:19: Make known to us what we should say to Him; we cannot frame an argument because of darkness.
verses.37:20: Is it to be reported to Him that I would speak? Did a man ever say that he should be swallowed up?
verses.37:21: And now people cannot look at the light, brilliant as it is in the skies, after a wind has passed over and cleared them.
verses.37:22: From the north a golden radiance comes; upon God is awesome majesty.
verses.37:23: As for the Almighty, we cannot find Him; He is great in strength, and He does not violate justice and abundance of righteousness.
verses.37:24: Therefore people fear Him; He has no regard for any who are wise in heart."
verses.38:1: Then the LORD answered Job from the storm and said,
verses.38:2: "Who is this darkening counsel with words lacking knowledge?
verses.38:3: Now gird your loins like a strong man; I will question you, and inform Me.
verses.38:4: Where were you when I founded the earth? Declare, if you know understanding.
verses.38:5: Who set its dimensions, since you know, or who stretched a line across it?
verses.38:6: Upon what were its pedestals sunk, or who laid its cornerstone,
verses.38:7: while the stars of morning rang out together and all the sons of God raised a joyful shout?
verses.38:8: And who hedged in the sea with double doors when it gushed out, emerging from the womb,
verses.38:9: when I set a cloud as its clothing and dense darkness as its swaddling cloth,
verses.38:10: and prescribed My boundary for it, and set a bar and double doors,
verses.38:11: and said, 'Up to here you shall come, and go no further; and here the pride of your waves shall be halted'?
verses.38:12: Ever since your days began, have you commanded the morning and made the dawn know its place,
verses.38:13: to grasp the edges of the earth so that the wicked are shaken from it?
verses.38:14: It is transformed like sealing clay, and they stand out like clothing.
verses.38:15: And from the wicked their light is held back, and a lifted arm is broken.
verses.38:16: Have you come as far as the wellsprings of the sea, and walked about in the recesses of the deep?
verses.38:17: Have the gates of death been uncovered to you, and do you see the gates of deep shadow?
verses.38:18: Have you discerned the full breadths of the earth? Declare, if you know all of it.
verses.38:19: Where is the way to where light dwells, and as for darkness, where is its place,
verses.38:20: so that you might take it to its boundary and understand the paths to its house?
verses.38:21: You know, since you were born back then, and your days are many in number!
verses.38:22: Have you come to the treasuries of snow, and have you seen the treasuries of hail,
verses.38:23: which I have kept in reserve for a time of distress, for a day of battle and war?
verses.38:24: Where is the way along which light is distributed, and the east wind spreads out over the earth?
verses.38:25: Who has split open a channel for the downpour, and a way for the bolt of thunder,
verses.38:26: to send rain on a land with no man, a wilderness with no human in it,
verses.38:27: to satisfy waste and desolation, and to make shoots of fresh grass sprout?
verses.38:28: Is there a father for the rain, or who has fathered the drops of dew?
verses.38:29: From whose womb did the ice emerge, and as for the frost of heaven, who gave birth to it?
verses.38:30: Waters hide themselves like stone, and the face of the deep locks together.
verses.38:31: Can you tie the chains of the Pleiades, or untie the cords of Orion?
verses.38:32: Can you bring out Mazzaroth in its season, and lead the Bear along with her children?
verses.38:33: Do you know the statutes of heaven, or can you set its rule upon the earth?
verses.38:34: Can you raise your voice to the cloud so that a deluge of water covers you?
verses.38:35: Can you send out lightning bolts so that they go and say to you, 'Here we are'?
verses.38:36: Who placed wisdom in the inner depths, or who gave the mind understanding?
verses.38:37: Who can count the clouds with wisdom, and who can tip the waterskins of heaven,
verses.38:38: when dust runs into a hardened mass and clods are stuck together?
verses.38:39: Can you hunt prey for a lion, and fill the appetite of young lions,
verses.38:40: when they crouch in the dens, waiting in the thicket in ambush?
verses.38:41: Who prepares its provision for the raven when its young cry out to God for help, wandering with no food?"
verses.39:1: "Do you know the time the wild goats of the rock give birth? Do you watch the birthing of the does?
verses.39:2: Can you count the months they complete, and do you know the time of their giving birth?
verses.39:3: They crouch down, they deliver their young, and they cast off their birth pangs.
verses.39:4: Their offspring grow sturdy, they grow large in the open country; they go out and do not come back to them.
verses.39:5: Who sent the wild donkey out free, and who untied the tethers of the onager,
verses.39:6: for whom I set the arid plain as its house, and the salt land as its dwellings?
verses.39:7: It laughs at the uproar of the city; it does not hear the shouts of a driver.
verses.39:8: The range of the mountains is its pasture, and it seeks after all greenery.
verses.39:9: Will a wild ox be willing to serve you, or spend the night beside your feeding trough?
verses.39:10: Can you tie a wild ox in a furrow with its rope, or will it harrow valleys behind you?
verses.39:11: Will you rely on it because its strength is immense, and leave your toil to it?
verses.39:12: Will you be confident in it that it will bring back your grain and gather it in at your threshing floor?
verses.39:13: The ostrich's wing beats with joy, yet are her pinion and plumage caring?
verses.39:14: For she leaves her eggs to the ground and warms them upon the dust,
verses.39:15: and she forgets that a foot might crush them, and a beast of the field tread them down.
verses.39:16: She acts harshly toward her young, as though not hers; her toil is for nothing, without fear,
verses.39:17: for God has caused her to forget wisdom and has not allotted her a share in understanding.
verses.39:18: The moment she raises herself up high, she laughs at the horse and its rider.
verses.39:19: Do you give might to the horse? Do you clothe its neck in a mane?
verses.39:20: Do you cause it to leap like the locust? The majesty of its snorting is terror.
verses.39:21: It paws in the valley and revels in strength; it goes out to meet weaponry.
verses.39:22: It laughs at fear and is not terrified, and it does not turn away before a sword.
verses.39:23: Against it rattles a quiver, the flash of spear and javelin.
verses.39:24: With quaking and fury it swallows up the ground, and it will not hold still at the sound of a horn.
verses.39:25: Whenever the horn sounds, it says, 'Aha!' And from a distance it smells war, the thunder of commanders and the battle shout.
verses.39:26: Does a hawk take wing by your understanding, spreading its wings toward the south?
verses.39:27: Or is it at your command that an eagle rises high and sets its nest aloft?
verses.39:28: It dwells on a rock and lodges overnight, upon a spur of rock and a stronghold.
verses.39:29: From there it searches out food; its eyes gaze from afar.
verses.39:30: And its fledglings lap up blood, and wherever the fallen are, there it is."
verses.40:1: Then the LORD answered Job and said,
verses.40:2: "Will a reprover dispute with the Almighty? Let the one who argues with God answer it."
verses.40:3: Then Job answered the LORD and said,
verses.40:4: "Look, I am small; what can I reply to You? I have put my hand over my mouth.
verses.40:5: Once I have spoken, and I will not answer; and twice, and I will not continue."
verses.40:6: Then the LORD answered Job from a storm and said,
verses.40:7: "Now gird your waist like a man; I will question you, and you inform Me.
verses.40:8: Will you indeed invalidate My justice? Will you declare Me guilty so that you may be in the right?
verses.40:9: Or do you possess an arm like God, and with a voice like His can you thunder?
verses.40:10: Adorn yourself now with grandeur and loftiness, and clothe yourself in splendor and majesty.
verses.40:11: Pour forth the outbursts of your anger; look upon every proud one and bring him low.
verses.40:12: Look upon every proud one, subdue him, and crush the wicked where they stand.
verses.40:13: Hide them together in the dust; bind up their faces in the hidden place.
verses.40:14: Then even I will praise you, that your right hand can deliver you.
verses.40:15: Look now at Behemoth, whom I made alongside you; he eats grass like cattle.
verses.40:16: Look now: his strength is in his loins, and his vigor is in the muscles of his belly.
verses.40:17: He stiffens his tail like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are intertwined.
verses.40:18: His bones are pipes of bronze; his limbs are like an iron bar.
verses.40:19: He is the foremost of the ways of God; let the One who made him bring near His sword.
verses.40:20: For the mountains bear produce for him, and all the wild animals of the field play there.
verses.40:21: Beneath the lotus trees he lies down, in the hiding place of reeds and marsh.
verses.40:22: The lotus trees screen him as his shade; the willows of the stream encircle him.
verses.40:23: If a river surges, he does not panic; he stays confident though the Jordan bursts against his mouth.
verses.40:24: Can anyone capture him before his eyes, or pierce his nose with snares?
verses.40:25: Can you haul out Leviathan with a fishhook, or force down his tongue with a rope?
verses.40:26: Can you place a reed-cord in his nose, or pierce his jaw with a barb?
verses.40:27: Will he multiply pleas for mercy to you, or will he speak gentle words to you?
verses.40:28: Will he cut a covenant with you? Will you take him as a slave forever?
verses.40:29: Will you play with him like a bird, or tie him up for your girls?
verses.40:30: Will partners barter over him? Will they portion him out among merchants?
verses.40:31: Can you fill his hide with barbed spears, or his head with a fishing harpoon?
verses.40:32: Place your hand upon him; remember the battle—do not do it again!"
verses.41:1: "Look, hope of him proves false; is one not thrown down even at the sight of him?
verses.41:2: No one is fierce enough to rouse him; and who is he who can take his stand before Me?
verses.41:3: Who has given to Me beforehand, so that I should repay? Everything under all the heavens belongs to Me.
verses.41:4: Concerning him, shall I keep silent about his limbs, and the account of mighty strength, and the grace of his proportion?
verses.41:5: Who has uncovered the surface of his garment? Who can enter within his double bridle?
verses.41:6: Who has opened the doors of his face? Surrounding his teeth is terror.
verses.41:7: His pride is rows of shields, closed up as with a tight seal.
verses.41:8: One draws close against another, and no air can enter between them.
verses.41:9: Each is bonded fast to the next; they interlock and cannot come apart.
verses.41:10: His snorts make light flash, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the dawn.
verses.41:11: From his mouth torches go forth; sparks of fire shoot out.
verses.41:12: From his nostrils smoke comes out, like a fanned cauldron and rushes.
verses.41:13: His breath sets coals ablaze, and a flame comes out from his mouth.
verses.41:14: In his neck strength resides, and before him dismay leaps.
verses.41:15: The folds of his flesh adhere together; cast solid upon him, it cannot be shaken.
verses.41:16: His heart is cast solid like a stone, and cast solid like a lower millstone.
verses.41:17: At his rising, the mighty are terrified; at the crashings, they lose their bearings.
verses.41:18: If a sword reaches him, it cannot hold—neither spear, nor dart, nor lance.
verses.41:19: He considers iron as straw, and bronze as decayed wood.
verses.41:20: No arrow can put him to flight; for him, stones of a sling are turned into stubble.
verses.41:21: Clubs are considered like stubble, and he laughs at the whirring of a javelin.
verses.41:22: Beneath him are sharp potsherds; he spreads a threshing sledge over the mud.
verses.41:23: He causes the depths to boil like a pot; the sea he makes like an ointment pot.
verses.41:24: Behind him he lights up a path; one would consider the deep to have white hair.
verses.41:25: Upon the earth he has no equal, one made without dread.
verses.41:26: He looks upon everything lofty; he is king over all the children of pride."
verses.42:1: And Job answered the LORD and said,
verses.42:2: "I know that You are able to do all things, and no plan can be withheld from You.
verses.42:3: 'Who is this who conceals counsel without knowledge?' Therefore I declared, though I did not understand, things too marvelous for me that I did not know.
verses.42:4: 'Hear, please, and I will speak; I will question you, and you inform Me.'
verses.42:5: By the hearing of the ear I had heard of You, but now my eye has seen You.
verses.42:6: For this reason I recant and repent in dust and ashes."
verses.42:7: Now it happened, after the LORD had spoken these words to Job, that the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, "My anger burns hot against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken what is right concerning Me, as My servant Job has.
verses.42:8: And now, take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to My servant Job, and offer up a burnt offering on your behalf; and Job, My servant, will pray for you, for I will surely receive him favorably, so as not to deal with you as your folly deserves, because you have not spoken what is right concerning Me, as My servant Job has."
verses.42:9: Then Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did just as the LORD had spoken to them, and the LORD received Job favorably.
verses.42:10: And the LORD restored Job's fortunes as he prayed on behalf of his friends, and the LORD increased everything that belonged to Job to twice as much.
verses.42:11: Then all his brothers and all his sisters and all who had known him previously came to him, and they ate bread with him in his house. They sympathized with him and comforted him over all the calamity that the LORD had brought on him, and each of them gave him one piece of money, and each one a gold ring.
verses.42:12: And the LORD blessed Job's latter days more than his beginning, and he came to have fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand pairs of oxen, and one thousand female donkeys.
verses.42:13: And he had seven sons and three daughters.
verses.42:14: He called the name of the first Jemimah, the name of the second Keziah, and the name of the third Keren-happuch.
verses.42:15: No women as beautiful as the daughters of Job were found in the entire land, and their father gave an inheritance to them among their brothers.
verses.42:16: And Job lived one hundred and forty years after this, and he saw his sons and his grandsons, four generations.
verses.42:17: Then Job died, aged and full of days.

notes.1:5: Hebrew uses the Piel of barak ("bless") as a pious euphemism for "curse" when God is the object (likewise in 1:11, 2:5, and 2:9).
notes.1:6: Hebrew ha-satan carries the definite article, designating a role or title ("the adversary" or "the accuser") in the heavenly assembly.
notes.1:10: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv has the defective spelling at, while the read qere attah gives the standard masculine singular pronoun "You."
notes.1:22: Literally, "did not give impropriety [or unsavoriness] to God" (Hebrew tiphlah).
notes.2:3: Hebrew levalle'o (Piel infinitive construct of bala') literally means "to swallow him up," an idiom for utter ruin; chinnam ("for nothing") directly echoes Satan's question in 1:9.
notes.2:7: Ketiv/Qere: the written ketiv reads 'ad ("to"), while the read qere adds the conjunction we'ad ("and to" / "even to").
notes.2:8: The Hithpael infinitive construct lehithgared ("to scrape himself") is the only occurrence of the root garad in Biblical Hebrew.
notes.3:3: The passive Pual perfect horah ("has been conceived") is the sole Pual form of harah in Biblical Hebrew, paired with gever ("male" / "man," here a male child).
notes.3:5: Qal yig'aluhu comes from ga'al ("reclaim" as kinsman-redeemer, or possibly a homonym meaning "defile"). Masoretic tsalmavet vocalizes "shadow of death" (often analyzed etymologically as "deep gloom"), and kimrire yom ("blacknesses of day") is a hapax legomenon usually linked to a root meaning "grow dark."
notes.3:6: Following the Masoretic pointing, Qal jussive yichad derives from chadah ("rejoice," as in Exod 18:9); some ancient versions and modern translations revocalize to yechad from yachad ("be joined").
notes.3:10: Hebrew literally reads "the doors of my womb" (bitni), referring idiomatically to the womb that conceived and bore him (parallel to "his day" in 3:1).
notes.3:20: Active Qal yitten ("does He give") has no explicit subject here, anticipating "God" (Eloah) in 3:23; some render it impersonally ("is light given"). In 3:23, "hedged around" (wayyasekh ... ba'ado) ironically echoes Satan's words in 1:10.
notes.4:6: Hebrew yir'atekha is literally "your fear," used absolutely for reverence toward God. The second clause is chiastic with a poetic postponed conjunction ("your hope, and the blamelessness of your ways").
notes.4:10: The opening phrases lack a separate verb in Hebrew, governed by poetic ellipsis or zeugma with the final verb nitta'u, a hapax Niphal perfect of nata' (a by-form of natats, "break out" or "knock out").
notes.4:17: The preposition min on "God" and "his Maker" is rendered in its standard comparative sense ("more righteous than ... purer than"), though it can also be understood relationally ("righteous before ... pure before").
notes.4:19: The phrase lifney-'ash is literally "before a moth," an idiom expressing extreme fragility, as easily crushed as or sooner than a moth.
notes.4:21: Hebrew yitram ("their cord") refers here to a tent cord, matching the Niphal verb nissa' ("pulled up," used of striking camp); some render the homograph "their wealth" or "their remainder."
notes.5:3: The Masoretic Text reads the first-person Qal verb wa'eqqov ("and I cursed," from naqav), expressing Eliphaz's immediate pronouncement of doom upon the fool's dwelling.
notes.5:5: The Masoretic vocalization tsammim is a masculine singular noun meaning "snare" (as in Job 18:9), governing the singular verb sha'af ("pants after"); some translations emend it to tseme'im ("the thirsty").
notes.5:6: Hebrew 'awen ("iniquity") repeats the term from 4:8 alongside 'amal ("trouble") and carries a dual nuance encompassing both wrongdoing and the affliction that accompanies it.
notes.5:7: Hebrew beney-reshef ("sparks") is literally "sons of flame," an idiomatic expression for rising sparks, linked to the first clause by a comparative conjunction ("just as").
notes.5:24: Hebrew lo' tekheta' uses the Qal imperfect of khata' (ordinarily "sin") in its concrete primary sense of "miss the mark" or "find something missing" when inspecting one's property.
notes.6:2: The qere reads wehawwati ("and my calamity," from hawwah), whereas the ketiv reads wehayyati, a morphological by-form from hayyah with the same meaning.
notes.6:6: The Hebrew hapax legomenon challamut (lit. "slime of challamut") is uncertain; modern lexicons generally identify it as a bland mucilaginous plant such as purslane or mallow, while the Targum and rabbinic tradition render it "the white of an egg."
notes.6:14: Following the Masoretic Text lammas ("to the despairing/melting one," from mss), with the second clause taken concessively ("even if he forsakes"); the Vulgate and Peshitta read a form of m's ("one who withholds kindness from his friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty").
notes.6:21: Following the provided Masoretic Text reading lo ("nothing," a substantivized negative); a qere tradition in some manuscripts reads lo ("to it" or "like it," referring to the dry wadi).
notes.6:29: The qere reads weshuvu ("and turn back," Qal masculine plural imperative of shuv), whereas the ketiv reads weshuvi (either "and my turning/reply" or a feminine singular imperative).
notes.7:1: The qere reads the poetic preposition aley ("upon") for the ketiv al (same meaning); tsava ("hard service") denotes conscripted military or forced labor.
notes.7:4: The phrase umiddad-erev takes middad as a Piel perfect of mdd ("the evening stretches out"); some connect the form to ndd ("flee") as continuing the question, "and when will the evening pass away?"
notes.7:5: The qere reads wegush ("and a clod/crust," a biblical hapax legomenon) for the ketiv wegish (same meaning); raga means either "hardens/crusts over" or "cracks," followed by Niphal wayyimma'es (from m's II, "dissolves/oozes").
notes.7:20: The Masoretic Text reads alay ("to myself"), which rabbinic tradition lists among the scribal corrections (tiqqune soferim) for an original aleykha ("to You"), reflected in the Septuagint.
notes.8:14: The rare Qal verb yaqot (from qut II) means "snaps" or "is cut off." "A spider's house" translates literal bet akkabish (a spider's web), setting up the wordplay with "his house" in v. 15.
notes.8:17: Hebrew yehezeh (Qal of hazah) literally means "gazes upon" or "sees," paired with literal "house of stones" (echoing "house" in vv. 14-15); some scholars instead connect the verb with a cognate root meaning "grasps" or "clings to."
notes.8:19: The Masoretic accents divide the second clause as "and from the dust | others will sprout," taking singular aher ("another") collectively with the plural verb yismahu ("will sprout"); without that division, the phrase could be read "from another dust they will sprout."
notes.8:21: Hebrew ad here functions adverbially like od ("still" or "yet"), and the Piel verb yemalleh is spelled with a final he instead of alef (for standard yemalle, "fill").
notes.9:9: The Hebrew star names ash, kesil, and kimah are traditionally identified as the Bear (Ursa Major), Orion, and the Pleiades, while "the inner chambers of the south" refers to the constellations of the southern sky.
notes.9:15: The unique Poel participle meshopeti ("my judge") denotes one acting as judge or legal opponent against Job; "plead for favor" (Hithpael of hanan) echoes Bildad's exact verb in 8:5.
notes.9:19: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "summon me" (Hiphil of ya'ad with first-person singular suffix), either asking who can summon Job to a fair hearing or echoing God's unspoken challenge ("Who can summon Me?"); ancient versions such as the Septuagint read a third-person suffix ("summon Him").
notes.9:30: Following the qere (read text) "with snow water" (beme-sheleg); the ketiv (written text) uses the poetic preposition bemo, reading "with snow" (bemo-sheleg).
notes.9:35: The terse Hebrew clause literally reads "for not so am I with myself," meaning either that Job's own conscience does not hold him guilty, or that as matters currently stand with him he cannot speak free of dread.
notes.10:7: The Hebrew prepositional phrase al-da'tekha (lit., upon Your knowing) functions concessively here, meaning even though You know.
notes.10:15: The form ure'eh can be parsed either as a construct verbal adjective (gazing on, parallel to the construct adjective seva, filled with) or as a Qal imperative (and look upon my affliction).
notes.10:20: Translated from the Masoretic Qere (read forms) wachadal (cease) and weshit (and turn away), both Qal imperatives; the Ketiv (written forms) read third-person imperfects yechdal and yashit (let him cease ... let him turn away).
notes.10:22: The feminine Hiphil verb wattopa (shine forth, echoing v. 3) has land as its subject, expressing the paradox that its very shining is pitch darkness. The noun tsalmaweth is vocalized by the Masoretes as shadow of death, though many linguists derive it from a root meaning deep darkness.
notes.11:6: The dual noun kiflayim (twofold) depicts sound wisdom as multifaceted and deep. The Hiphil verb yasheh (from nshh, cause to forget) with partitive min indicates that God overlooks or remits part of Job's iniquity.
notes.11:11: The clause welo yithbonan (Hithpolel of byn, consider or take notice) is taken as an unmarked rhetorical question (will He not take notice?), though some construe it circumstantially (without needing to investigate).
notes.11:12: The Hebrew plays on navuv (Qal passive participle, hollow) and the denominative Niphal yillavev (from lev, heart or mind, meaning gain understanding). The conjunction we- introduces a proverbial impossibility (when the colt of a wild donkey is born a human), though some take it concessively.
notes.11:17: The Masoretic vocalization ta'ufah reflects a Qal imperfect with paragogic -ah from 'wf (be dark), yielding even if it grows dark; some interpreters revocalize it as a noun meaning gloom.
notes.12:4: The Hebrew shifts from first-person singular ehyeh (I have become) to third-person appositional forms (lere'ehu, to his friend; wayya'anehu, and He answered him), casting Job's plight in proverbial third-person terms.
notes.12:5: Reading the Masoretic consonants lpyd as le-fid (for misfortune or calamity, cf. Job 30:24; 31:29), with contempt as the masculine subject of stands ready; the Masoretic vocalization lappid reads a despised torch in the thought of one at ease.
notes.12:6: The final clause la'asher hevi eloah beyado is syntactically difficult; parallel to the preceding le- phrases, it literally reads to the one who brings a god in his hand (making his own might his god), though some take God as subject (to whom God brings provision by His hand).
notes.13:8: Show favoritism renders the Hebrew idiom literally meaning 'lift up His face' (similarly in v. 10), denoting judicial partiality.
notes.13:15: The Ketiv reads lo ('not', i.e., 'I have no hope' or 'I will not wait'), whereas the Qere translated here reads lo ('in Him', i.e., 'in Him I will hope').
notes.13:16: Hebrew hu can refer either to the preceding circumstance ('This too', translated here) or directly to God ('He also will be my deliverance').
notes.13:27: Hebrew literally reads 'around the roots of my feet' (an idiom for the soles or footprints), with the Hithpael verb indicating carving or tracing a boundary line.
notes.13:28: The abrupt third-person pronoun 'he' refers to Job himself or to frail humanity in general, bridging into the lament of chapter 14.
notes.14:3: The Masoretic Text has the singular 'Your eye' and shifts abruptly to the first-person object 'me' rather than third-person 'him'.
notes.14:6: The Qal verb ratzah here can mean 'complete / pay off' a term of service (as in Lev 26:34; Isa 40:2) or 'enjoy / take pleasure in' one's day.
notes.14:14: Hard service (tzava) denotes compulsory or military duty, pairing with 'relief' (chalifah, also 'renewal' or 'replacement', cognate with the Hiphil verb 'sprout again' in v. 7).
notes.14:16: Continuing the wish of vv. 13-15, ki-attah ('for then') and the negative clause depict God ceasing to track Job's sin; alternatively, taking ki-attah as 'for now' and the second clause as an unmarked rhetorical question ('do You not watch over my sin?'), vv. 16-17 describe God preserving Job's sins as evidence.
notes.14:19: Hebrew seficheha ('its torrents', from a root denoting pouring out or scattering) is a rare poetic plural construed with a feminine singular verb, with its suffix referring back to the waters.
notes.15:12: The verb yirzemun ("are flashing") is a hapax legomenon, likely related by metathesis to Aramaic rmz ("wink, blink, signal with the eyes") and denoting defiant or agitated flashing of the eyes.
notes.15:22: The Ketiv reads the defective form wspw, while the Qere reads the Qal passive participle wesapuy (from sph, "watch, spy out"), translated here as "spied out" (that is, watched and marked out for the sword).
notes.15:24: The noun kidor ("onslaught") is a hapax legomenon of uncertain etymology, commonly understood from context and Semitic cognates as "battle," "attack," or "onslaught."
notes.15:29: The hapax legomenon minlam ("their possessions") is generally derived from a root meaning "acquire" or "attain," with a third-person plural suffix shifting collectively to the wicked (as in 15:35).
notes.15:30: The suffix on "His mouth" (piw) is generally understood to refer to God's mouth (cf. 4:9), though some take it as the wicked man's own speech.
notes.16:5: The noun nid ("sympathy") is a hapax legomenon from the root nwd ("move, shake, show condolence"), permitting either an ironic sense ("mere movement of my lips") or "sympathy/condolence"; the verb yahsok ("bring relief") is used elliptically without an explicit object, anticipating the same root in 16:6.
notes.16:8: The verb qmt ("shriveled"), occurring only here and in 22:16, can mean either "shrivel/wrinkle" or "seize/bind"; paired with kahashi ("my gauntness/leanness"), it pictures Job's wasted body testifying against him.
notes.16:16: The Ketiv reads the feminine singular verb hmrmrh, whereas the Qere reads the plural Pealal verb homarmeru ("are inflamed") to agree grammatically with the plural noun panay ("my face").
notes.16:20: The Hiphil participle melisay ("my mockers") derives from lys, which can mean either "scorn/mock" (cf. Ps 119:51) or "interpret/mediate" (cf. 33:23); in apposition to reay ("my friends"), "my mockers" fits the contrast with Job's tearful appeal to God.
notes.16:21: The Hiphil verb weyokah ("that one might plead") has an unspecified third-person singular subject—either the heavenly witness of 16:19 or an indefinite "one"—followed by a comparative waw in the second clause ("as a son of man [pleads] for his friend").
notes.17:3: The opening combines two Qal imperatives, literally "put down, please" (simah-na) and "stand surety for me" (arveni), with an implied object ("a pledge"). The Niphal verb yittaqa ("strike hands," lit. "be struck into my hand") refers to the legal gesture of clapping hands to seal a guarantee (cf. Prov 6:1).
notes.17:5: This terse proverb uses yaggid (Hiphil of ngd, "denounce, inform against," cf. Jer 20:10) with leheleq, meaning "for a share" of spoil or reward, though some derive heleq from the homonym meaning "smoothness, flattery."
notes.17:6: Literally "and a spitting to faces (tophet lephanim) I have become," taking the hapax noun tophet as "spitting" (cognate with Aramaic tuph, "to spit"), meaning one spat in the face.
notes.17:16: The feminine plural verb teradnah ("will go down") either serves as an archaic singular form with feminine tiqvati ("my hope," v. 15) or refers to Job's hopes collectively. Masoretic nahat is the pausal noun ("rest" or "descent"), rather than a revocalized 1cp imperfect nehat ("we shall descend").
notes.18:2: The hapax qintsei is an Aramaizing plural construct of qets ("end") with nasalization, matching the Aramaic plural millin ("words"), though some connect it to an Arabic root meaning "hunt" or "snare." Bildad addresses Job using 2mp forms in vv. 2-3.
notes.18:3: The Niphal perfect nitminu derives from tmh ("be stopped up, dull, senseless"), though it may also be a by-form of tma ("be regarded as unclean").
notes.18:12: Hebrew letsalo can mean either "for his fall/stumbling" (tsela II, as in Ps 38:18, which pairs the same noun with nakon) or "at his side" (tsela I).
notes.18:15: Masoretic mibbelilo is written as one word fused from mibbeli-lo ("what does not belong to him," lit. "of not-to-him"), with the 3fs verb tishkon ("dwells") taking an indefinite neuter subject or anticipating feminine gophrit ("sulfur").
notes.19:17: The verb hannoti is Qal perfect 1cs of hnn II ("be loathsome, foul-smelling"), though traditional exegesis sometimes links it to hnn I ("my pleading"). Literally "sons of my womb" (benei vitni), referring either to full brothers born of the same womb (cf. 3:10) or to Job's own kin.
notes.19:26: Hebrew weahar ori niqqephu-zot (lit. "and after my skin they have stripped off this") uses an impersonal 3cp Piel of nqp II ("cut off, strip away, destroy") with deictic zot ("this"). The preposition in mibbesari ("from my flesh") can denote vantage point ("from/in my flesh") or separation ("apart from my flesh").
notes.19:27: Literally "my kidneys (kilyotai) fail in my bosom (beheqi)," the Hebrew anatomical idiom for one's deepest emotions and longing.
notes.19:28: The Masoretic text reads nimtsa-vi ("is found in me"), shifting from direct quotation into Job's own perspective; some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions read bo ("in him").
notes.19:29: Ketiv shdyn (shedin) vs. Qere shaddun (relative particle sha, "that," prefixed to dun, a by-form of din, "judgment"); both the written and read forms yield "that there is a judgment."
notes.20:10: The verb yerassu (Piel of rasah) means "seek the favor of, appease," and 'ono here denotes "his wealth" or "his substance" (contrast 21:19).
notes.20:18: Literally, "according to the wealth of his exchange, and he will not exult," meaning he derives no joy from all the proceeds of his trading.
notes.20:23: The noun lahumo ("his food," fitting "fill his belly") can also mean "his flesh" (cf. Zeph 1:17); the poetic suffix on 'alemo here has singular reference ("upon him").
notes.20:26: The verb yera' is the Qal imperfect of ra'a' ("fare badly, come to ruin") with "what remains" as subject; some instead take it from ra'ah ("graze, consume") with "fire" as subject.
notes.20:29: Literally, "the inheritance of his word" (or "decree"), using the suffix objectively for the lot appointed for him by God.
notes.21:13: Ketiv reads yblw ("they wear out/spend," Piel of balah); Qere reads yekallu ("they finish/complete," Piel of kalah). The verb yehattu is Qal imperfect of nahat ("go down, descend").
notes.21:19: The first clause echoes the friends' conventional objection as a rhetorical question, and 'ono here comes from 'awen ("iniquity" or "punishment for iniquity").
notes.21:24: The rare plural noun 'atinayw occurs only here in Biblical Hebrew and is understood as "his pails/vats" (matching the vocalized halab, "milk"), though some connect it with body parts such as "his sides" or "his flanks."
notes.21:30: With the preposition le-, the Niphal yehasek ("be held back, spared") and Hophal yubalu ("be led, carried") can mean either that the evil are spared on the day of disaster and carried safely away on the day of wrath, or that they are reserved for the day of disaster and led forth to the day of wrath.
notes.21:32: The noun gadish (elsewhere "grain stack") here denotes a "burial mound" or "tomb," and the 3ms imperfect yishqod ("keeps watch") is used impersonally ("watch is kept").
notes.22:2: The poetic suffix -מוֹ on עָלֵימוֹ here refers to a singular antecedent ("himself," i.e., the discerning man), though some take it as "to Him" (God).
notes.22:17: MT reads third-person לָמוֹ ("to them" or "for them"), shifting abruptly from the first-person מִמֶּנּוּ ("from us"); some ancient versions harmonize this to "to us."
notes.22:24: בֶּצֶר (also in v. 25) is a rare term for gold ore; MT reads כְּצוּר ("as stones/rock") rather than בְּצוּר ("among the stones").
notes.22:29: The Hebrew כִּי־הִשְׁפִּילוּ וַתֹּאמֶר גֵּוָה is terse: Hiphil הִשְׁפִּילוּ can be read impersonally ("when people are brought low"), and גֵּוָה means either "lifting up" or "pride." שַׁח עֵינַיִם is literally "bowed of eyes" (humble or downcast).
notes.22:30: MT reads אִי־נָקִי ("one who is not innocent"), using the rare negative particle אִי (cf. 1 Sam 4:21); יְמַלֵּט (Piel) and נִמְלַט (Niphal) pair active and passive forms of מלט ("rescue").
notes.23:2: MT reads יָדִי ("my hand") rather than "His hand" (found in the Septuagint and Syriac), and מְרִי literally means "rebellion/rebellious" (from מרה), though some take it as "bitter."
notes.23:9: The four directional terms in vv. 8-9 (forward, backward, left, right) also serve as the four compass points (east, west, north, south). אָחַז is an apocopated Qal imperfect 1cs of חזה ("see/glimpse"), and יַעְטֹף can mean either "He turns" or "He conceals Himself."
notes.23:12: MT reads מֵחֻקִּי ("more than my allotted portion," i.e., daily food or prescribed measure; cf. Prov 30:8), whereas the Septuagint and Vulgate read "in my bosom" (בְּחֵיקִי).
notes.23:17: The Hebrew is difficult; this translation takes נִצְמַתִּי (Niphal of צמת, "be cut off") with מִפְּנֵי ("before") and extends the negative לֹא across the second clause, where כִּסָּה מִפָּנַי means "He concealed from my face." Alternatively, the verse can be read "Yet I am not silenced because of darkness, though thick gloom covers my face."
notes.24:6: Qere reads יִקְצוֹרוּ (Qal, "they reap"), whereas ketiv reads יקצירו (apparently Hiphil). MT בְּלִילוֹ ("his fodder") refers to the wicked landowner's crop, parallel to "the wicked" in the second clause.
notes.24:11: שׁוּרֹתָם can mean "their walls" or "their rows" (of olive trees); יַצְהִירוּ is a denominative Hiphil of צהר (from יִצְהָר, "fresh oil") meaning "press out oil."
notes.24:12: MT vocalizes מְתִים ("men") and תִּפְלָה ("wrong/folly"; cf. Job 1:22); some versions revocalize these to מֵתִים ("the dying") and תְּפִלָּה ("prayer").
notes.24:18: MT has no quotation marker ("You say") introducing vv. 18-24 and shifts between singular ("he") and plural ("their") pronouns referring collectively to the wicked.
notes.24:22: מָשַׁךְ (Qal of משׁך) here means "prolongs/sustains" (with God as implied subject, continuing into v. 23), though some render "drags off." בַּחַיִּין exhibits the Aramaizing plural ending -ִין.
notes.25:2: Hebrew hamshel ("dominion") is a rare substantive use of the Hiphil infinitive absolute of mashal ("to rule"), occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible.
notes.25:5: The verb ya'ahil ("shine") is the Hiphil imperfect of a rare root 'ahal ("be bright, shine"), distinct from the homonym "pitch a tent." The Qal perfect zakku ("are pure," from zakak) echoes the related verb yizkeh ("be pure," from zakah) in v. 4.
notes.26:4: Hebrew 'et-mi can be read either as "To whom" (marking the recipient of the Hiphil verb higgadta, "you have declared") or as the comitative preposition "With whom," meaning with whose assistance, paralleling "whose breath" in the second half.
notes.26:5: Hebrew harepha'im ("the shades") refers to the spirits of the dead in the underworld, and yecholalu ("writhe") is the Polal imperfect of chul/chil ("writhe, tremble in anguish").
notes.26:9: Masoretic kisseh ("throne") is an alternate spelling of kisse' (as in 1 Kings 10:19), though some modern versions repoint the consonants to read "full moon." The verb parshez ("spreads") is a unique quadriliteral form related to paras ("spread out").
notes.26:12: The translation follows the Qere uvitevunato ("and by His understanding") over the transposed Ketiv spelling. The Qal verb raga' ("stirred up") matches the exact phrase "stirs up the sea" in Isaiah 51:15 and Jeremiah 31:35, though many versions read it from a homonymous root meaning "stilled."
notes.26:14: The verb nishma' ("we hear") is morphologically ambiguous and can be parsed as either the Qal imperfect first-person plural ("we hear") or the Niphal perfect third-person singular ("is heard").
notes.27:8: The Masoretic Qal imperfect yivtsa' ("makes unjust gain") is taken actively with the godless man as subject, though some construe God as delayed subject ("when God cuts him off") or repoint it as a Niphal passive. The rare Qal form yeshel ("draws out") derives from nashal or shalah ("pull off, draw out").
notes.27:15: Hebrew bammawet yiqqaveru (Niphal, "will be buried by death") uses "death" poetically for deadly pestilence or personified Death serving as their sole burial.
notes.27:18: The Masoretic Hebrew reads ka'ash ("like the moth"), referring to a moth's fragile cocoon; the Septuagint and Syriac instead read "spider."
notes.27:19: The Masoretic Text reads the Niphal imperfect lo' ye'asef ("will not be gathered," meaning not gathered to his ancestors in honorable burial); the Septuagint and Syriac instead reflect a reading yosif ("will do so no more").
notes.27:23: Both 'alemo ("over him") and kappemo ("its palms") use the poetic suffix -emo alongside third-person singular verbs continuing the personified east wind from vv. 21-22, though some read the verbs impersonally of mocking onlookers.
notes.28:3: The unexpressed masculine singular subject in vv. 3-4 and 9-11 refers generically to the human miner rather than to God.
notes.28:4: The Masoretic Hebrew of this verse is notoriously obscure, using rare mining imagery: nachal (ordinarily a wadi or stream) here denotes a vertical shaft, meim-gar means literally "away from a sojourner/inhabitant," and dallu refers to miners dangling suspended by ropes.
notes.28:8: Hebrew benei-shachats means literally "sons of pride," a poetic idiom for majestic wild beasts.
notes.28:11: Hebrew mibbekhi means literally "from weeping," a poetic image for underground water seeping or trickling into mine shafts; the Piel verb chibbesh means "binds up" or "dams up."
notes.28:18: Hebrew meshekh (from the root "draw" or "pull") is uncertain here, denoting either the "possession" or "acquisition" of wisdom or possibly a "pouch" full of it.
notes.29:4: Hebrew bimei chorpi means literally "in the days of my autumn," using the fruitful harvest season as a metaphor for the prime of life; sod denotes God's intimate counsel or close fellowship.
notes.29:10: The Niphal plural verb nechbau (literally "hid themselves," here "was stilled") agrees grammatically by attraction with the plural noun "nobles" rather than the singular subject "voice."
notes.29:16: Hebrew rib lo-yadati places a construct noun directly before a verbal clause, meaning either "the dispute of one I did not know" (a stranger's case) or "a dispute I did not know."
notes.29:18: Hebrew chol ordinarily means "sand," though an ancient Jewish interpretive tradition renders it "phoenix," connecting it with the mention of a "nest" in the first line.
notes.29:24: The phrase lo yaaminu (literally "they did not believe") can mean either that those smiled upon could not believe such favor or that Job smiled at them when they lacked confidence.
notes.30:3: The Qal participle ha'orqim ("they gnaw") is alternatively derived from an Aramaic cognate meaning "flee" ("who flee to the parched ground"). Hebrew 'emesh literally means "last night" and is taken poetically here as "by night" or "in gloom."
notes.30:11: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere (read form) is yitri ("my cord" or "my bowstring"), whereas the Ketiv (written form) is yitro ("his cord" or "his bowstring").
notes.30:17: Night (laylah) is construed as the subject of the active Piel verb niqqar ("pierces"). The form 'orqay ("my gnawing pains") may alternatively derive from a cognate noun meaning "my sinews" or "my veins."
notes.30:22: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere (read form) is tushiyyah ("substance," "security," or "sound wisdom"), construed with Polel temogegeni as "melt away my substance." The Ketiv (written form) tshwh is commonly read as "roaring storm" or "crash."
notes.30:24: This verse is famously difficult in the Masoretic Text; shalach yad be- ("stretch out a hand against") is taken as an idiom for striking a helpless "heap of ruins" ('i). Many interpreters alternatively read the clause as a rhetorical question describing a falling person reaching out for help in disaster.
notes.31:11: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere (read form) reads feminine hi' agreeing with zimmah ("depravity") and masculine wehu' agreeing with 'awon ("iniquity"), whereas the Ketiv (written form) reverses the two pronouns.
notes.31:15: The indefinite numeral 'echad ("One") serves as the subject of the Polel verb wayekhunennu ("fashioned us"), emphasizing that the same Creator formed both master and servant in the womb.
notes.31:18: The Qal verb gedelani ("he grew up with me") carries an indirect-object suffix referring to Job caring for the fatherless child from youth, parallel to Hiphil 'anchennah ("I guided her") referring to the widow.
notes.31:26: Hebrew 'or literally means "light" and here denotes the sun in parallel with yareach ("moon").
notes.31:33: Hebrew ke'adam lacks the definite article and may mean either "like Adam" (alluding to Genesis 3) or generically "as humans do."
notes.32:4: The Hebrew clause literally reads "waited for Job with words," an unusual construction with the Piel of chakah followed by the direct object marker, indicating that Elihu held back from speaking while Job and the older men spoke.
notes.32:9: Hebrew rabbim literally means "the great" or "the many," here denoting those senior in years or standing, parallel to "elders" in the second clause.
notes.32:21: The Piel verb akhanneh, repeated in 32:22, literally means to bestow an honorific surname or flattering title, hence to flatter.
notes.33:7: The noun akhpi, "my pressure," is a hapax legomenon related to the verb akhaph, "press" or "urge," in Proverbs 16:26; the Masoretic Text is followed here rather than the Septuagint reading "my hand."
notes.33:13: Literally "He does not answer any of His/his matters (or words)." The third-person suffix may refer either to God's own doings and words, or back to "a mortal" in 33:12, meaning He answers none of a mortal's words.
notes.33:19: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads rov, "the multitude of" his bones, translated here with "pain" carried over from the first clause, whereas the Ketiv reads riv, "strife" in his bones is continual.
notes.33:21: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads the Pual verb shuppu, "are laid bare," translated here, whereas the Ketiv reads shephi, a noun form meaning "bareness" or a singular form.
notes.33:28: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads third-person naphsho and chayyato, "his soul" and "his life," translated here as a third-person summary, whereas the Ketiv reads first-person naphshi and chayyati, "my soul" and "my life," continuing the quotation from 33:27.
notes.34:6: The Piel imperfect 'akhazzev ("I lie") is rendered as an unmarked rhetorical question ("Am I to lie?"); some interpret it passively as "am I treated as a liar?" Also, chitsi literally means "my arrow," a metonymy for an arrow-inflicted wound (cf. 6:4).
notes.34:18: The Masoretic Text points ha'emor as the interrogative particle plus Qal infinitive construct ("should one say?"), treated here as a parenthetical question. Ancient versions and many translations revocalize it as a participle (ha'omer, "who says") referring to God.
notes.34:23: The Qal imperfect yasim ("sets") is used elliptically for "sets the heart/attention" (cf. 23:6; 34:14), and the Masoretic Text reads 'od ("further"), indicating God requires no further investigation. Some emend 'od to mo'ed ("appointed time").
notes.34:29: Verses 29-30 have abrupt, elliptical syntax in Hebrew, literally "and over a nation and over a person alike, from the reigning of a godless person, from snares of the people." The Hiphil yashqit ("remains silent") can also be taken transitively as "gives quietness."
notes.34:36: The opening word 'avi is an obscure optative particle probably derived from the root 'avah ("desire, wish"), hence "If only" or "My wish is."
notes.35:2: The preposition in me'el ("than that of God") is comparative, echoing Elihu's earlier charge that Job justified himself rather than God (32:2). Some read me'el as "before God" or "from God."
notes.35:3: The Hebrew shifts from second-person singular lach ("to you") to first-person singular 'o'il ("I gain") and mechattati ("from my sin"), moving abruptly from indirect or generic speech into Job's direct voice; some take lach as addressed to God ("to You"). The phrase mechattati is a concise comparison meaning "more than if I had sinned."
notes.35:15: Hebrew pash ("insolence") is a hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning, often linked to a root meaning "arrogance" or "excess"; many translations conjecturally emend it to pesha' ("transgression"). Also, 'ayin ("not") rarely negates a finite verb here (paqad 'appo, "His anger has punished").
notes.36:16: The Hebrew syntax is compressed: "lured you" renders the Hiphil perfect of sut (echoed in 36:18), "in place of it" reflects tachteha (lit. "beneath/instead of it"), and "what rested" renders nachat (from nuach, "rest").
notes.36:18: The opening Hebrew clause is elliptic (lit. "for wrath, so that it not lure you"), and the rare noun sepeq (from sapaq, "slap/clap") can mean "scoffing/derision" or alternatively "a blow" or "abundance."
notes.36:19: Hebrew shua can mean either "cry for help" (matching the verb in 36:13) or "wealth/opulence," and the concise phrase lo vetsar (lit. "not in distress") follows the Masoretic vocalization for tsar ("distress").
notes.36:30: Hebrew or literally means "light," used poetically in storm contexts here and in 36:32, 37:3, 37:11, and 37:15 to denote lightning.
notes.36:33: This verse is notoriously difficult in Hebrew; "its crashing" renders reo (from rua, "shout/roar"), while "livestock" (miqneh) and "what is rising" (oleh, Qal participle of alah, "ascend," referring to the rising storm) follow the Masoretic vocalization strictly.
notes.37:6: The imperative heve ("fall" or "be") uses an Aramaic-influenced form of the root hawah, and the doubled phrase "downpour of rain, even the downpour of His mighty rains" follows the Masoretic vocalization of uzzo ("of His might") as a noun with suffix rather than a verb.
notes.37:7: Following the Masoretic construct plural anshei, kol-anshei maasehu literally reads "all the people of His making" (those He has created), though some interpret it as "that all people may know His work."
notes.37:9: "The chamber" (hacheder) likely alludes to the southern storehouse of tempests (cf. Job 9:9), and mezarim ("scattering winds," a hapax Piel participle of zarah, "scatter") traditionally denotes the cold north winds.
notes.37:16: The hapax noun miflesei ("balancings," from palas, "weigh/balance") creates deliberate wordplay with mifleot ("marvels"), and "the One complete in knowledge" echoes Elihu's own phrase in 36:4.
notes.37:22: "A golden radiance" translates Hebrew zahav (lit. "gold"), used metaphorically for the bright golden glow of the northern sky or divine splendor.
notes.38:1: Ketiv writes מנהסערה as a single word; Qere divides it into two words (מִן הַסְּעָרָה, "from the storm"), which is followed in the translation.
notes.38:11: Literally "and here one sets [a limit] against the pride of your waves"; the Qal imperfect יָשִׁית ("sets") is used impersonally to express halting the surging sea.
notes.38:12: Ketiv reads ידעתה שחר (placing the ה on the verb as an archaic 2ms ending); Qere divides it as יִדַּעְתָּ הַשַּׁחַר ("made the dawn know"), using a rare Piel perfect of יָדַע ("cause to know").
notes.38:30: יִתְחַבָּאוּ is a Hithpael of חָבָא ("hide themselves"), depicting water concealed under a stone-hard crust of ice (though some lexicons posit a homonym meaning "harden"), parallel to the reciprocal Hithpael יִתְלַכָּדוּ ("lock together").
notes.38:36: Both טֻחוֹת ("inner depths / inward parts", cf. Ps 51:6 [MT 51:8]) and the hapax legomenon שֶׂכְוִי ("mind", from שׂכה "perceive") are rare and debated; some interpret them instead as meteorological or animal terms ("cloud layers" and "rooster").
notes.39:8: MT vocalizes יְתוּר as a noun ("range" or "territory", from תּוּר "explore/roam"), translated literally here; many translations repoint it as a verb ("ranges").
notes.39:12: Ketiv reads Qal ישוב ("will return", intransitive); Qere reads Hiphil יָשִׁיב ("will bring back", transitive with זַרְעֶךָ, "your grain"), followed in the translation.
notes.39:13: The feminine adjective חֲסִידָה ("caring / kind", modifying absolute אֶבְרָה "pinion") is also the Hebrew name for the stork, creating wordplay contrasting the caring stork with the neglectful ostrich.
notes.39:19: The hapax legomenon רַעְמָה derives from רָעַם ("quiver / thunder") and is generally understood as the horse's quivering mane, though ancient versions often rendered it literally as "thunder".
notes.39:21: MT reads the plural verb יַחְפְּרוּ ("they paw", referring generically to horses or to the hooves) before shifting immediately to singular verbs (וְיָשִׂישׂ, יֵצֵא); smoothed to singular "It paws" for English flow.
notes.40:2: Hebrew harov combines the interrogative particle with the Qal infinitive absolute of riv ("dispute/contend") functioning as a finite verb, paired with the rare noun yissor ("reprover/faultfinder," from yasar).
notes.40:6: Ketiv writes mns'rh as one word without a space; Qere divides it into two words, min se'arah ("from a storm"), followed here.
notes.40:17: The Qal verb yahpots (from a rare root chaphats II, distinct from "delight in") is lexically uncertain, meaning either "stiffens" or "bends."
notes.40:19: The second clause (literally "the One who made him brings near His sword") may mean either that only God can approach Behemoth with His sword, or that God supplied Behemoth with his own sword-like weapon.
notes.41:4: Qere reads lo ("concerning him," translated here as an unmarked rhetorical question introducing the description in vv. 5-26); Ketiv reads lo' ("not": "I will not keep silent about his limbs").
notes.41:5: Masoretic Hebrew literally reads "within his double bridle" (be-khefel risno), a poetic figure for Leviathan's jaws; the Septuagint reads "breastplate/armor."
notes.41:7: Masoretic Hebrew reads ga'avah ("pride") with afiqey maginnim ("rows/channels of shields"); some ancient versions presuppose "his back."
notes.41:17: Hebrew elim can mean "the mighty" or "gods/divine beings." The Hithpael verb yitchatta'u (from chata', normally "purify oneself") is taken here in its base root sense of "miss the way / lose one's bearings" amid the crashings (shevarim, likely breaking waves).
notes.41:20: Hebrew literally reads "son of a bow" (ben-qashet), a poetic idiom for an arrow.
notes.42:2: Ketiv reads yd't, an archaic or defective first-person spelling without final yod or second-person "You know"; the translated Qere reads yada'ti (Qal perfect 1cs, "I know").
notes.42:4: Job here quotes the LORD's exact challenge from 38:3 and 40:7 ("I will question you, and inform Me"), paralleling his citation of 38:2 in 42:3; some instead read the verse in Job's own voice addressing God ("I will ask You, and inform me").
notes.42:6: The Qal imperfect verb em'as ("reject, despise") has no explicit object in Hebrew and is understood either as withdrawing Job's words ("I recant") or reflexively ("I despise myself"). Niphal nihamti ("repent, relent") can also mean "be comforted," leading some to translate "and I am comforted concerning dust and ashes."
notes.42:8: Hebrew "lift up his face" (repeated in 42:9) is an idiom for receiving someone favorably and granting their intercession. Literally "not to do folly with you," the following phrase means either not to treat the friends as their folly deserves or not to inflict disgrace on them.
notes.42:10: Ketiv reads shevit ("captivity"), while the translated Qere reads shevut ("fortunes/restoration"), a standard Hebrew idiom with shuv for reversing an afflicted state. The noun re'ehu ("his friend") is a collective singular referring to Job's friends.

unplaced.text: For He will fulfill what is decreed for me, and many things like these are with Him.
unplaced.note: Hebrew literally reads "my decree," meaning the portion allotted to me, and "with Him" refers to what He holds in His purpose.
